stories.title: Managing energy, water constraints critical to Australia's AI ambitions
stories.summary: Industry experts argue Australia's AI ambitions hinge on how policymakers manage the energy and water demands of new data centers, advocating regulation that targets the efficiency of technology deployed inside facilities. Smarter rules on cooling and compute efficiency could curb power and water strain without stalling sector growth. The comments come as data center proposals multiply across Sydney and Melbourne.
stories.why_it_matters: The regulatory approach Australia chooses will determine how quickly projects can connect to the grid and access water, directly affecting hyperscalers and developers planning APAC capacity. A technology-focused framework could become a model for other water- and power-constrained markets in the region.
stories.content:
# Managing energy, water constraints critical to Australia's AI ambitions

Wed, 2nd Sep 2026 (Today)

Australian policymakers are being urged to take a more sophisticated approach to regulating data centre efficiency as the country prepares for a significant increase in electricity demand.

This is the view of Matt Oostveen, Vice President & Chief Technology Officer, APJ for Everpure.

Talking exclusively to TechDay, in the lead up to Everpure's "ANZ Accelerate" conference in Melbourne on September 30, Oostveen suggested that Australia's federal and state governments should look beyond the energy performance of facilities and focus on the technology operating inside them.

They should also consider the broader implications for the nation's economy, technological development and data sovereignty, he said.

As forecasts point to a sharp rise in electricity consumption, the debate around the construction of new data centres needs to be one of balance - considering the amount of power and water they consume, and the positive economic benefits to the nation.

Australian stakeholders need to understand why the infrastructure is being built in the first place, he outlined.

"Australia is water constrained. It is power constrained, but we need to understand why we're making these things and what the purpose is behind it," Oostveen said.

The economic opportunity created by the infrastructure extends far beyond the facility itself.

"The employment opportunity isn't inside the facility," he said.

"There are some jobs in there for tech workers, but this is about the broader Australian economy. This is about us participating in an international AI revolution and being a player there."

The growth of AI and increasingly data-intensive technologies has accelerated demand for computing and storage infrastructure around the world.

For Australia, the expansion of local data centres is also being driven by the need to retain greater control over sensitive information.

Data sovereignty is one of the major reasons behind the shift.

"Geopolitics has changed," Oostveen said, noting that Australian companies are increasingly questioning who ultimately has jurisdiction over the data has stored on cloud infrastructure, particularly where providers were headquartered in foreign countries.

If a foreign court has jurisdiction over data stored in an Australian data centre, that raises question marks over sovereignty.

Industries including healthcare, government and financial services have particularly strong reasons to consider where sensitive information was stored, and which legal systems could potentially apply to it.

Australia's growing data requirements are also being shaped by 'data gravity' - the increasing cost and complexity of moving vast volumes of information between systems and jurisdictions.

As businesses place data at the centre of their technology architectures, applications, AI systems and other computing resources are increasingly being brought closer to where that information is stored.

"That new data-centric world is starting to emerge," Oostveen said.

"Where are we going to keep the data? We're going to put it inside data centres."

But Australia needs to ensure the expansion of the sector doesn't place unnecessary strain on electricity and water infrastructure.

Recent forecasts have raised concerns about the rapid growth in power demand from data centres, with some projections suggesting the sector's share of electricity consumption could rise significantly over the next decade.

The debate, however, should not simply focus on whether new power generation or new data centres were required. Policymakers should also examine opportunities to reduce the energy consumption of the technology deployed inside those facilities.

Everpure estimates that storage infrastructure accounts for approximately 20–25 per cent of the energy consumed within a data centre.

Much of that infrastructure continues to rely on mechanical hard drives, creating an opportunity to significantly reduce energy consumption through denser and more efficient storage technologies.

"If Australian data centres were to switch to technology as dense as ours, you could shrink that 25 per cent number to around two per cent," Oostveen said.

"Rather than building new energy stations, rather than having to construct new data centres, because there's also a smaller footprint that's contained in such dense materials, we can probably be driving a 10-times improvement just on that storage layer alone."

Existing approaches to data centre efficiency have been too heavily focused on high-level measurements of an entire facility.

Metrics such as power usage effectiveness, or PUE, remained useful for assessing overall performance, but regulators should also examine the efficiency of the servers, storage and other infrastructure operating on the data centre floor.

Oostveen cited Singapore, where he is currently based, as an example of a market where policymakers have begun taking a more detailed approach.

"Singapore is one of the few countries in the world that's actually mandating for the efficiency of the infrastructure that sits on that data centre floor," he said.

"Everyone else looks at it from a holistic perspective, but they are taking a bottom-up approach as well as a top-down approach."

Australia could adopt a similar model and establish standards that measure the amount of energy required to provide a certain amount of data storage.

We now have an opportunity to establish best practice through legislation, but the clock is ticking.

The aim should be to encourage data centre operators and technology suppliers to continually reduce the amount of energy required by underlying infrastructure rather than focusing on the overall energy consumption of an increasingly large facility.

Oostveen also suggested that some public discussion risks presenting an incomplete picture of how the facilities operate and the benefits they could provide to Australia.

"Now is the time for cool, calm heads to cut through with facts and be able to explain to people exactly what these facilities are, how they work, and what to expect from them," he said.

"The benefits for younger Australians are profound. The benefits for the Australian economy are strong."

stories.title: Mirantis k0rdent AI gains NVIDIA hypervisor certification
stories.summary: Mirantis has secured NVIDIA hypervisor certification for its k0rdent AI platform, validating near-bare-metal GPU performance within about five percent in virtualized environments. The certification enables cloud operators to partition and share expensive GPU resources across tenants more efficiently. It applies to NVIDIA's virtualized GPU stack used in AI infrastructure.
stories.why_it_matters: GPU scarcity makes utilization the key economics lever for AI cloud providers, and certified virtualization removes the performance penalty that previously pushed operators toward dedicated bare metal. Neoclouds and enterprises can squeeze more revenue and workloads from the same hardware.
stories.content:
# Mirantis k0rdent AI gains NVIDIA hypervisor certification

Wed, 2nd Sep 2026 (Today)

Mirantis' k0rdent AI platform has been certified through NVIDIA's Certified Hypervisors programme, covering GPU virtualisation for enterprise AI factories and cloud service providers.

The validation followed benchmarking tests designed to measure how closely virtualised GPU performance matched bare-metal deployments. In those tests, k0rdent AI delivered performance within 5% of comparable bare-metal systems across validation scenarios on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and NVIDIA HGX-based tracks.

GPU virtualisation allows organisations to divide computing resources more precisely between workloads instead of assigning an entire GPU server to one user or project. The approach is becoming more relevant as companies and cloud operators look to share expensive AI infrastructure across multiple teams while keeping performance losses low.

Mirantis is among the first independent software vendors to join the NVIDIA-Certified Hypervisors programme. The certification builds on the company's earlier involvement in NVIDIA's AI Cloud Ready validation work, which focused on AI infrastructure deployment.

For companies building AI systems, the certification is intended to reduce the engineering work needed to design, test and run production GPU virtualisation. It also gives customers an external benchmark for software intended to support shared AI environments.

### Shared infrastructure

The shift toward multi-tenant AI infrastructure has increased demand for software that can isolate workloads securely while using hardware efficiently. In practice, that means allowing different users or customers to run jobs on the same underlying systems without giving them full access to an entire server.

In Mirantis' approach, virtual machines serve as the security boundary, with networking, GPUs and storage isolated for each customer or workload. This operating model mirrors what many large AI cloud environments require.

The platform also manages both virtual machines and Kubernetes workloads through a single control plane. That allows organisations to run AI models, databases, traditional business applications and supporting services on the same management layer rather than maintaining separate stacks for virtualisation and container orchestration.

A key part of the platform is its topology-aware scheduler, designed to understand how GPUs, CPUs, network interfaces and storage are connected inside a server and across a rack. Mirantis says this allows workloads to be placed with awareness of NVIDIA NVLink fabrics, NUMA domains and NVIDIA InfiniBand or RoCE networking, reducing bottlenecks that could affect AI training and inference.

### Market context

The announcement reflects a wider effort across the AI infrastructure market to increase utilisation of GPU systems, which are costly and often in short supply. Cloud providers and enterprise operators are under pressure to allocate these resources more efficiently while preserving the speed needed for large-scale model training and inference.

Near bare-metal performance has become a key metric in that effort because many AI workloads are sensitive to latency and bandwidth constraints. Any virtualisation layer that introduces too much overhead can undermine the economics of shared infrastructure.

Mirantis says its software was built for AI factories and cloud providers that need flexible GPU allocation, workload isolation and operational efficiency across several teams or tenants. It argues those requirements are becoming more common as AI infrastructure shifts from dedicated systems to pooled environments.

Kevin Kamel, Vice President of Product Management at Mirantis, said the certification showed the software could support that transition.

"As AI infrastructure evolves into shared, multi-tenant AI factories, organizations need virtualization that delivers flexibility without sacrificing performance," said Kevin Kamel, Vice President of Product Management at Mirantis. "This certification demonstrates that k0rdent AI enables enterprises and cloud providers to securely virtualize NVIDIA accelerated infrastructure while maintaining the performance required for AI training and inference workloads."

### Product availability

Mirantis said k0rdent AI Virtual Machine as a Service is available as a technical preview. It sits alongside other parts of the company's infrastructure software, including Bare Metal as a Service, Kubernetes orchestration and AI infrastructure management tools.

The company sells Kubernetes-based infrastructure software for enterprise customers and has positioned k0rdent AI as part of a broader push into the market for shared GPU clouds and enterprise AI deployments. Its customer list includes Adobe, Ericsson, Inmarsat, MetLife, PayPal and Societe Generale.

The latest certification gives Mirantis another credential as competition intensifies among software providers building management layers for GPU-heavy infrastructure, with performance, isolation and ease of operation emerging as the main points of comparison.

stories.title: Four of Vietnam's subsea cables suffer faults, leading to fresh connectivity outages for country
stories.summary: Four of Vietnam's submarine cable systems have developed faults simultaneously, causing fresh internet connectivity outages across the country. The incident repeats a pattern seen several times in recent years, when multiple concurrent cable breaks degraded Vietnam's international bandwidth. Repair timelines depend on vessel availability and weather conditions.
stories.why_it_matters: Recurring multi-cable failures expose Vietnam's fragile international connectivity, a direct risk for cloud regions, content delivery, and any data center investment thesis built on Vietnamese demand. It strengthens the case for new cable landings and route diversity, and for enterprises to plan redundancy across borders.
stories.content:
Vietnam has once again been plagued by multiple subsea cable outages.

As reported by VN Express, four of the six subsea cables that connect the country have suffered disruptions due to multiple simultaneous faults within these cables, though the specifics of these faults have not been revealed.

Vietnam is connected by six undersea fiber-optic cable systems: AAG, IA, AAE-1, APG, ADC, and SJC2, with the last two being the newest cables.

The cables impacted include parts of the SJC2 cable, which connects the country to other parts of Asia; the AAE-1 cable, which has seen issues since February; the Asia-America Gateway (AAG), which connects Southeast Asia with the US; and the Intra Asia (IA) cable have also seen issues. Repairs on the AAG and IA cables are expected to start this month.

The SJC2 cable is the latest to suffer disruption, notes VN Express, which reports that the cable developed a fault in its S4 segment near Chung Hom Kok, Hong Kong, last week.

These faults have led to mobile network operators in the country reporting network disruption, including VNPT and Viettel, while around 30 percent of Vietnam's international Internet traffic.

In order to navigate these challenges, Viettel has added 800Gbps of international connectivity via the IA cable on Wednesday, and is also adding 300Gbps through the Asia Pacific Gateway.

It's not the first time the country's subsea cables have suffered severe disruption. In 2024, three cables connecting Vietnam (IA, APG, and AAE-1) were all hit by outages, while a year earlier, all five cables that connected the nation at the time were down simultaneously.

stories.title: AWS launches Graviton5-powered R9g cloud instances
stories.summary: AWS has introduced R9g instances powered by its fifth-generation Graviton5 Arm processor, delivering up to 25 percent more compute per vCPU for memory-intensive workloads such as databases and analytics. The launch extends AWS's custom-silicon strategy across its general-purpose and memory-optimized families. The instances are available in select regions with broader rollout to follow.
stories.why_it_matters: Each Graviton generation deepens AWS's price-performance advantage and reduces dependence on x86 vendors, pressuring Intel and AMD's cloud share. For customers, it lowers the cost of data-heavy workloads; for competitors, it raises the bar on custom silicon investment.
stories.content:
# AWS launches Graviton5-powered R9g cloud instances

Wed, 2nd Sep 2026 (Today)

Amazon Web Services has made its Amazon EC2 R9g and R9gd instances generally available. The new instances use AWS Graviton5 processors.

The launch expands AWS's line-up of Arm-based cloud servers for memory-intensive workloads, with the new range positioned as an upgrade to the earlier R8g generation.

R9g is the standard memory-focused version, while R9gd adds local NVMe-based solid-state storage for workloads that need low-latency local access. The new instances target databases, in-memory caches, analytics workloads and Linux-based applications, including containerised services.

R9g delivers up to 25% higher compute performance per virtual CPU than Graviton4-based R8g instances, according to AWS. The company also cited faster DDR5 memory, a larger L3 cache, and higher networking and Amazon EBS bandwidth on the largest sizes.

The top-end 48xlarge configuration offers up to 100 Gbps of network bandwidth and up to 72 Gbps of EBS bandwidth, according to published specifications. AWS is offering both the standard virtualised format and a metal version for customers that want direct access to the full physical server.

Each of the R9g and R9gd families is available in 11 sizes, from medium to metal-48xl. The largest options provide 192 vCPUs and 1,536 GiB of memory, placing the range in the market for large databases, caching layers and memory-heavy analytics systems.

Storage is one of the main distinctions between the two variants. R9g instances are EBS-only, while R9gd includes local NVMe SSD storage ranging from 59 GB on the smallest size to three 3,800 GB drives on the largest systems.

### Hardware changes

AWS said Graviton5 introduces several hardware changes over Graviton4, including DDR5 memory running at 8,800 MT/s, a fivefold increase in L3 cache size, and up to three times higher packet-processing performance.

The largest instance sizes can also provide up to twice the network and EBS bandwidth of the previous generation, according to AWS. That matters for customers running distributed databases or analytics clusters where memory size alone is not enough to avoid network bottlenecks.

Another feature in the new families is Instance Bandwidth Configuration, which lets customers adjust the split between Amazon EBS and Amazon VPC networking bandwidth by 25%. AWS said this is designed for workloads with specific bandwidth needs, including databases and caching applications.

### Security focus

All R9g and R9gd instances run on the AWS Nitro System, the company's server architecture that moves virtualisation, storage and networking functions onto dedicated hardware. The new instances also include the Nitro Isolation Engine, which AWS introduced earlier this year with its C9g and M9g ranges.

AWS said the Nitro Isolation Engine enforces separation between virtual machines and controls access to memory, CPU register state and I/O devices through a limited set of interfaces. The company added that the component uses formal verification methods to demonstrate that it behaves as intended.

This work forms part of a broader AWS push to make security and isolation a more visible selling point in its infrastructure products, particularly as more customers place sensitive workloads on shared cloud systems. AWS said the Nitro system is the first cloud hypervisor to be formally verified.

### Migration path

Customers already running workloads on R8g instances should be able to move to equivalent R9g sizes without code changes in most cases, according to AWS. Supported operating systems include Amazon Linux 2023, Amazon Linux 2, Ubuntu 22.04 and later, RHEL 8.4 and later, SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 15 SP3 and later, and Debian 12 and later.

The new instances also support Amazon EKS, Amazon ECS and standard Kubernetes deployments for containerised workloads. Applications built for Arm64 container images can run without modification, according to AWS.

At launch, the instances are available in US East in Northern Virginia and Ohio, US West in Oregon, and Europe in Frankfurt. Customers can buy them through On-Demand, Spot, Savings Plans, Dedicated Instances and Dedicated Hosts.

Published specifications show that the entry-level r9g.medium starts with 1 vCPU and 8 GiB of memory, while the equivalent r9gd.medium adds 59 GB of local NVMe storage. At the other end of the range, the r9gd.48xlarge and r9gd.metal-48xl include three 3,800 GB NVMe SSDs alongside 192 vCPUs and 1,536 GiB of memory.

The release adds another tier to AWS's Graviton-based portfolio as the cloud provider continues to steer customers towards its in-house Arm processors for general, compute and memory-intensive workloads.

stories.title: Flying the Flag for subsea connectivity in the AI era
stories.summary: The subsea cable operator formerly known as GCX has rebranded as Flag and is refocusing its strategy on serving AI data center connectivity demand. The company operates extensive submarine and terrestrial fiber assets across Asia, the Middle East, and beyond. Its repositioning targets the bandwidth surge between AI compute hubs and global networks.
stories.why_it_matters: AI traffic is reshaping subsea economics, and incumbent carriers are retooling to capture inter-data-center demand rather than legacy wholesale. For hyperscalers planning APAC and Middle East capacity, carriers like Flag become critical partners or competitors in securing diverse, high-capacity routes.
stories.content:
In September, it will be four years since Flag (Fibre Links Around the Globe) came back from the dead.

The subsea cable operator, then known as Global Cloud Xchange (GCX), had filed for bankruptcy in 2019 with debts of $350 million. In 2021, GCX reemerged, before being snapped up by investment firm 3i Infrastructure in September 2022 for $512 million.

“I've been at Flag now for six years as of July, when it had just come out of bankruptcy,” says Carl Grivner, CEO, Flag. “Since then, we reshaped it, rebuilt it, and then we sold it to a private equity firm here in London.”

Flag owns one of the world’s largest private subsea fiber optic networks and provides end-to-end high-speed digital connectivity solutions, including colocation capacity, dark fiber, and Layer 2 and 3 services for hyperscalers, telcos, OTT content providers, and enterprises across its interconnected platform of seven subsea and six terrestrial cable systems.

## Planting the Flag

A part of the company’s revival has been its rebrand, which was announced in April of last year. Flag’s previous name was a point of contention, Grivner says.

“It’s quite comical,” he laughs. “The original name was Global Cloud Xchange, which was then translated into GCX… a lot of the OTT players hated it,” explains Grivner. “It was a ‘wait a minute, you're not in the cloud business and not in an exchange in any way, so why are you called GCX?’ It was a painful discussion to have.”

It’s from here that Flag was the obvious choice, says Grivner, who noted the name’s prominence within the industry resonates with people.

The company now shares its name with several of its subsea cables, including the FLAG Europe-Asia, FLAG-Atlantic, and FLAG North Asia Loop systems.

“We decided to go back to Flag, which was a historical and very successful brand in the industry,” says Grivner. “When you’re at events, it seems like everybody worked at Flag at one point or another. People cherish the little memorabilia, such as the pins you put on your jacket, or the silly socks that say Flag and things like that.”

Grivner knows a thing or two about what makes a successful brand. He was previously CEO of Colt Technology Services for four-and-a-half years, and has also served as chief executive of Singapore-based telco Pacnet.

## Growing out its terrestrial focus

In total, Flag’s subsea cable network covers 66,000km (41,010 miles), from North America to Asia. It offers capacity on the FA-1, HAWK, Falcon, MEDEX, FEA, IEX, and FNAL systems, and operates and/or arranges capacity at cable landing stations in Taiwan, Japan, France, the UK, and the US, as well as offering modular data center services.

Last year, Flag also acquired capacity on Google’s Echo cable, snapping up a fiber pair on the route that connects Singapore to the US via landing stations at Eureka, California; Piti, Guam; and Changi, Singapore.

Grivner explains that while the company’s focus has traditionally been subsea cable routes, there’s more of an interest to grow out its terrestrial footprint. Those fiber assets link the company’s subsea assets directly to terrestrial networks, data centers, and cable landing stations across Europe, the Middle East, and Asia.

“The business right now is about 90 percent subsea and 10 percent terrestrial, and we're changing that model to about 60-40,” he adds, pointing to the opportunities that lie in the data center market.

“We’re currently adding routes in Iraq and Saudi Arabia, and we'll continue to add more terrestrial routes as we see fit.” He argues that this will provide data centers in the region with more redundancy.

According to Paul Abfalter, chief strategy and revenue officer at Flag, the end of 2026 will have seen the company invest $250 million since being acquired by 3i Infrastructure in 2022, with the cash spent on Flag’s network and new capabilities.

“With 3i’s leadership, we’re looking to dramatically change the way that the business is architected from the network architecture point of view, as well as obviously investing in a whole bunch of new systems and capabilities to make it a bit more ready for the AI era,” explains Abfalter.

## AI demands reshape subsea connectivity

Since joining the company in 2020, the backdrop of the telecoms world has changed, explains Grivner, with the focus shifting from cloud to AI.

“I've been around technology for a long, long time, and I've seen different waves come and grow,” he says. “Around the 2020 time-frame, a lot of the growth from a Flag perspective was driven by cloud and the rollout of cloud. And in the last 24 months, it's been driven by AI.”

The emergence of AI has led to a huge demand for subsea cable capacity.

According to Grivner, AI workloads have altered expectations and demands for bandwidth, claiming that this demand is up 10 times compared to a cloud perspective.

“The AI boom is here,” Grivner says. “It's an arms race amongst all of the providers to come up with the best latency, the response times, the redundancy, the diversity, the capacity in terms of network, and we're at the beginning of that.”

Adding to this, Abfalter says that the demand for AI is putting pressure on the need to develop more routes, such as inter-region routes, rather than focusing necessarily on just long-haul networks.

## Route diversity

The need for more cable capacity ties into the need for more diverse connectivity. The changing geopolitical landscape means offering a variety of routes has never been more important.

While subsea cable operators such as Flag have always had to contend with accidental damage to their cables, there are more severe challenges to deal with. Recent instability in the Middle East has brought this discussion to the fore, with various technology companies seeing their infrastructure across parts of the region attacked. Data centers have been targeted in parts of the region, with facilities operated by AWS and Oracle apparently being hit by drone strikes.

The unrest is being closely monitored by the subsea cable industry as well, with ocean infrastructure regularly targeted as a means of disrupting communications, particularly as uncertainty continues around the Strait of Hormuz, which has been subject to various barricades and threats of military action.

“We have not seen any impact to connectivity at this point in time,” Grivner tells *DCD* when asked if Flag has noted any consequences of the war. The company has cables spanning parts of the Middle East, including its Falcon and FEA routes.

While the disruption has been minimal so far, the conflict has highlighted the need for route diversity, adds Grivner, who says the need for a ‘Plan B’ route is essential for customers.

“There’s a need for diversity and redundancy in the Middle East right now, with the concerns about different locations being threatened or weakened,” says Grivner.

“With the diversity of routes that we're built, building in from a terrestrial perspective, we have ways of circumventing if a break were to happen in a particular location, I think that's going to be the norm. That's why I say I don't think anybody's going to be purely a subsea business anymore. I think the balance between both subsea and terrestrial is going to be an important element of success moving forward.”

Abfalter tells *DCD* that the uncertainty in the region has paused building projects.

“The concern for us is that it slows down and pauses some of the build projects, including, obviously, some of the build projects in the Gulf and some of the projects that we're all working on, so that part is painful,” he says.

Flag is keen to plant its flag in more locations, with Grivner identifying further routes. He says that there are opportunities for more routes between Singapore and Australia to the US, plus demand for India to Europe, while intra-Asia will be important for the firm.

Grivner, however, does appear to rule out more routes across the Atlantic, for now.

“I haven't mentioned the Atlantic and won't,” he says. “We think our bread and butter is primarily in the other part of the world. I’m not saying the Atlantic is saturated, but we’re just seeing the demand from the other side of the world right now.”

Meanwhile, Abfalter anticipates that there are more terrestrial opportunities in the Middle East for Flag, notably in Saudi Arabia.

In June of last year, the company secured a $340m refinancing package, stating at the time it was “set to announce significant investments from Asia to Europe and throughout the Middle East."

“We're definitely seeing big investments in Saudi Arabia in making that terrestrial path happen, which will become the main path of the Red Sea,” he says. “We’re stepping up our presence in Iraq as well, and in Syria as things continue to stabilize there. You’re going to see that pop up as an important terrestrial market.”

## Middle Eastern Edge

It’s not just new routes that Flag is hoping to connect, the company has also got its eyes on expanding its Edge data center presence.

Flag owns and operates some small modular Edge data centers, including a deployment in Japan. The company declined to reveal publicly how many of these Edge data centers it operates. Grivner says that it hopes to build more of the data centers across the Middle East, in line with its plans to grow its presence in the region.

“We're looking to expand, with more of those in the Middle East,” he says. “We see this as part of the data sovereignty and [lower] latency opportunities,” he says. Given their modular nature, it is no surprise that Grivner says Flag’s upcoming data centers will not offer gigawatts of capacity. “They'll be in the 5MW-20MW size, modular units that we can build and transport to a customer location in just a few months,” he explains.

These Edge data centers offer an alternative to deploying the larger 100MW data centers that may not be appropriate for a certain location, as demand grows for data closer to the Edge.

When it comes to AI, Grivner says Flag needs to build for the future, while keeping pace with the rapid changes the industry is in the midst of.

“I used to say that telecoms was about 10 years ahead of its hype,” he adds. “Now it's more like 10 months ahead of its hype in terms of how fast things are rolling out.”

stories.title: Infleqtion supplies Japanese research team with QPU for neutral-atom quantum computer
stories.summary: Infleqtion has delivered a quantum processing unit to a Japanese research team building a neutral-atom quantum computer under the country's Quantum Moonshot program. The collaboration supplies core hardware for Japan's government-backed effort to achieve fault-tolerant quantum computing. Neutral-atom systems are one of several architectures Japan is pursuing in parallel.
stories.why_it_matters: Japan's state-funded quantum push is creating early demand for quantum hardware suppliers and the facilities that house them. For the data center sector, national quantum programs signal a future class of specialized, high-value compute infrastructure co-located with classical HPC.
stories.content:
Quantum computing firm Infleqtion has supplied a Japanese research team with a quantum processing unit (QPU) to support the launch of Japan’s first operational neutral-atom full-stack quantum system.

Dubbed Shunkai, the quantum computer is expected to initially operate with approximately 50 qubits, eventually scaling to 500 qubits as development of the system continues.

In its next phase, the team undertaking the Ohmori Moonshot project will focus on improving system integration, stability, and scalability. The quantum computer will be made available to external users across academia and industry to support the development of applications and advance quantum error correction research.

Professor Kenji Ohmori is leading the project at the Institute for Molecular Science (IMS), part of Japan’s National Institutes of Natural Sciences. Infleqtion was the only foreign quantum partner selected by the Japan Science and Technology Agency (JST) for its Quantum Moonshot program. Moonshot Goal 6 aims to build a fault-tolerant universal quantum computer and quantum Internet by 2050.

“This milestone marks a pivotal moment for Japan’s quantum ambitions as well as Infleqtion’s role in advancing production-ready quantum platforms at scale,” said Pranav Gokhale, chief technology officer at Infleqtion.

“Bringing a full-stack quantum system into production operation is a meaningful step toward fault-tolerant quantum computing that also serves as strong validation of neutral-atom architecture. Our quantum processing unit delivers the programmability, scalability, and fidelity control that next-generation systems demand.”

Founded as ColdQuanta and spun out from the University of Colorado in 2007, Infleqtion develops and designs instruments and systems for quantum technology applications.

In September 2025, the company announced plans to go public via a Special Purpose Acquisition Company (SPAC) merger with Churchill Capital Corp X. The company began trading on the New York Stock Exchange in February 2026, following the completion of the deal.

stories.title: DayOne partners with TNB to develop up to 1.5GW of onsite generation for planned data center in Selangor, Malaysia
stories.summary: DayOne has signed an agreement with Tenaga Nasional Berhad to develop as much as 1.5GW of onsite power generation and battery storage to serve a planned data center campus in Selangor. The arrangement signals a move toward self-supplied power in Malaysia's fast-growing data center hub, reducing reliance on constrained grid capacity. Details on the technology mix and timeline were not disclosed.
stories.why_it_matters: If executed, the deal would be one of Southeast Asia's largest behind-the-meter power commitments tied to a single data center project. It relieves pressure on TNB's grid, gives DayOne a faster and more certain path to energization, and sets a template other Malaysian developers may follow as grid connection queues lengthen.
stories.content:
APAC data center developer DayOne has partnered with TNB Power Generation, a subsidiary of Malaysian electrical utility TNB, to explore the development of an up to 1.5GW on-site generation solution for DayOne’s in-development data center in Selangor, Malaysia.

The partnership was formalized via a non-binding Memorandum of Understanding signed early last month. The on-site energy solution is expected to include both on-site generation and battery energy storage. The final capacity, configuration, and implementation model remain subject to feasibility assessments, definitive agreements, and applicable regulatory approvals.

“Malaysia is central to DayOne's growth, and we continue to deepen our presence in Greater Kuala Lumpur as we scale to meet accelerating AI and cloud demand. Together with TNB, we are exploring an integrated approach that combines on-site power generation and a battery energy storage system (BESS) directly with our data center infrastructure,” Jamie Khoo, CEO of DayOne, said. “This model is designed to add new capacity and enhance system flexibility that supports our growth while contributing to Malaysia's energy resilience and long-term sustainability.”

DayOne’s Selangor campus is in its early stages of development. The company acquired land for the facility last month from Malaysian property developer Mah Sing. The site spans 78.80 acres, with the deal expected to close in the second half of 2027.

APAC-focused DayOne was spun out of Chinese data center firm GDS back in 2025. The company's portfolio currently comprises more than 500MW of data center capacity in service and under construction, and more than 500MW held for future development across sites in Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia (Johor), Indonesia (Batam), and Japan (Tokyo).

Its deal with TNB builds on an existing relationship between the two firms. In June, DayOne signed a deal with the utility for 1.5GW of solar capacity and 2.2GWh of battery energy storage. This followed a deal for 500MW of solar power for two of its data centers in Malaysia, namely, Nusajaya Tech Park, in Gelang Patah, and Kempas Tech Park, in Johor Bahru, which combined have a capacity of 120MW.

stories.title: Bids land for Stack's $25b-plus data centres; MacCap lurks

stories.title: The Aussie AI Data Centre debate: profit, power & public trust
stories.summary: Australia's AI-driven data center expansion is drawing scrutiny over energy shortages, fears of an investment bubble, and growing community opposition, even as proponents project tens of billions of pounds in economic benefit. The debate pits the sector's profit potential against grid constraints and public trust concerns. Local backlash is beginning to affect project sentiment in key markets.
stories.why_it_matters: Community and political resistance is emerging as a real permitting risk for Australian data center projects, not just a communications issue. Developers and investors that fail to address power use and local benefit-sharing could face delays, tighter conditions, or blocked approvals.
stories.content:
# The Aussie AI Data Centre debate: profit, power & public trust

Tue, 1st Sep 2026 (Yesterday)

While technology issues do occasionally make it into political agendas, rarely does one transcend so many different political realms. The debates around AI cover everything from the environment and climate change to energy policy, infrastructure, town planning and personal ethics. With AI sitting at the nexus of multiple policy areas, it's not surprising that the debate can veer into the apparently chaotic.

### Data centre policy

The digital sector is now Australia's second-largest economic contributor behind mining, with the Productivity Commission estimating that AI will add around $116 billion to the economy over the next decade.

Federal Member for Casey Aaron Violi said "For decades, Australia's economic story has been defined by what we could dig out of the ground or grow from our soil. But today, technology presents to us an opportunity to grow a future not defined by our geography, but by our ability to adopt technology and scale it through the digital economy."

Reaping that harvest requires a regulatory and social environment that encourages investment. The Federal Government is planning to introduce legislation compelling data centre operators to completely offset all power consumption with renewables.

While National Cabinet agreed to work towards nationally consistent mandatory standards for large data centres, Queensland and the Northern Territory argued that states need flexibility to set energy rules tailored to their own communities and energy mixes.

While physical infrastructure is important, it's not the only consideration. Australia currently has some 285 data centres in operation with at least another 225 in planning and development. That will, inevitably, lead to increased load on the electricity grid. Coupled with the increased electrification of homes and transport, the grid must add generation and transmission capacity.

In its annually updated ten-year forecast, the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) said 14% of all power consumption will be from data centres in the coming years - up from around 3% today. While it's possible for that amount of generation and supporting infrastructure to be added, there is a challenge.

It takes less time to build a data centre and have it ready to operate than it does to build the energy generation it needs. While the federal government's intentions might be reasonable, it remains to be seen whether they're possible.

**Do we need that many data centres?**

The underpinning assumption of the data centre build is that large, centralised models will be the norm. But the ability to run smaller, bespoke models using on-prem hardware is rapidly increasing.

Kiraa AI co-founder Errol Brandt said there are about 1.5 billion AI capable devices made by Apple in the wild. And when the number devices made by other manufacturers is added, it brings into question whether the massive investment in large data centres is completely justified. Or at least, whether the apparent 'full speed ahead' mania we're seeing is completely justified.

Professor Toby Walsh from the University of New South Wales likens the speed at which data centres are being built with the massive investments made in fibre optics at the turn of the century.

"If you look at the $2T that were invested in fibre optics at the great fibre rollouts in the late 90s and early 2000s, that proved to be a bubble. The value of the telecom companies in the United States fell in value by about $2B, so it was mostly completely wiped out. And most of that fibre was dark for the first ten years because there was a huge over capacity. Today, that fibre's all lit and it's all being used to screen Netflix movies and the other stuff that we do, so it proved to be a reasonable long-term investment. But most of the money that was put in at the start was transferred from telecoms and people investing in telecoms to the companies now that are benefiting from it."

It's possible that we're seeing an overinvestment today and the companies and investors providing the funding today may not be the ones that receive the benefits.

Walsh posits that many of today's data centre investors are in the real estate business, and not the technology industry. As property speculators, they procure land and build, only to walk away when it's time for what he sees as inevitable need to inject more capital when technology advances in the future.

This may be behind Microsoft's pivot away from building its own AI data centres. Dr Joseph Sweeney, Advisor on the Future of Work at Australian analyst form Intelligent Business Research Services (IBRS), said the lack of profitability with the major AI players was a factor.

"What we're seeing already is AI infrastructure spending is now having to be offset. Microsoft, about two years ago, saw this coming and pivoted. They didn't stop building their own data centres, but they certainly postponed about $500B of them. And they started doing $5B investments with neoclouds for five-year contracts. Why would you do that? You do that because you realise that your overinvestment isn't going to pay off or maybe you're not sure if it's going to so you're hedging your bets. You're pushing up that financial risk."

**What if the AI bubble bursts?**

There has been massive investment by the Magnificent Seven which comprises Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet, Apple, Meta, Tesla and Amazon. But they are burning through cash faster than they can make it.

The sector is running at a loss. In June 2026, around $2.3 trillion has been wiped off the value of their collective enterprises.

And the market is maturing with a realisation that much of the value proposition offered by large AI providers is easily replicated.

"The problem is AI, or generative AI, or large language models or more specifically vector databases are an algorithm. You can't copyright them. You can't intellectually protect them in any way whatsoever," said Sweeney.

If what we are seeing is indeed a bubble, much like the dot com bubble, then the trillions of dollars invested in the Magnificent Seven and others may evaporate. That's not to say AI will disappear. But we'll see a groundswell of new players and possible some market consolidation.

We're already seeing some volatility in the market capitalisation of large AI companies with values rising and falling on the back of daily announcements.

"I suspect the same will be true of the investments into AI data centres that we will see a vast transfer of money from the people making those investments into the AI companies who eventually end up in the longer term using it," said Walsh.

### Public sentiment

Perhaps the biggest unknown facing the AI industry is how public sentiment impacts its uptake and the building of data centres. This is one of the areas the federal government intends to address through its new AI standards.

"The purpose of this standard is to make sure that we attract an outside share of global compute but do it in a way that maintains social license, avoids the backlash that we see in other in other countries and delivers real tangible benefits to Australians," said Andrew Charlton, the Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy.

Much of the AI debate is focussed on the construction of data centres and whether AI will result in significant unemployment.

When it comes to the impact on employment, one thing almost every expert agrees on is that, at the very least, there will be employment displacement. That is, while some roles will be automated out of existence, new jobs will be created.

Some of this debate echoes the use of industrial robots in automotive manufacturing. However, over time, the car industry employed more people. Routine and repetitive tasks were automated while higher value jobs evolved. It's possible we'll see the same happen with AI.

Data centre construction, however, has a very direct impact today on communities. While they do result in construction jobs – it can be difficult to hire an electrician for domestic work in some areas as many are engaged in data centre projects – once the construction is complete, these buildings require very few people for their operation.

Some of the public anger stems from the nature of the building process, as Walsh explained.

"Most of these data centres are sufficiently large planning applications that they don't require local consultation, and they go up to the state level. So, the public hasn't literally represented it. They're also right to be upset that they're being built in their backyard."

In Walsh's view there's no reason to build a data centre in residential areas. Given the speed data moves across fibre optic, you could build a data centre in a less populated area, such as where a former coal mine operated.

"As an example, to build a data centre in Lithgow, there's an older coal fired power station that they can close down. There are electric cables that go to Lithgow. I did the maths. It would take less than a millisecond for the electron to get from Lithgow to Sydney, which is a latency that most businesses would be happy with. I suspect the community would love the investment, would love to see the jobs, and would love to see something replacing that coal-fired power station that's going to be closed."

These construction decisions are building public distrust in AI as it coalesces with negative sentiment over data centre builds, energy use and the push towards renewables he added.

The debate over AI and its infrastructure highlights a core tension for Australia. There is the drive to harness a technology that could contribute up to $116 billion to the economy while simultaneously navigating the practical realities of energy supply, regulatory flexibility, and community impact.

The federal push for renewable‑offset data centres, paired with the National Cabinet's aim for mandatory standards, demonstrates an intent to balance growth with sustainability. Yet, the speed at which data centres can be erected contrasts sharply with the slower pace of adding grid capacity, raising legitimate concerns about whether the current investment trajectory is proportionate to the actual demand for large, centralised models.

Public confidence will ultimately shape the sector's trajectory. If data centre development is perceived as a top‑down process that bypasses local consultation and places environmental and economic burdens on small communities, the social licence to operate will erode.

A more measured approach that leverages smaller, bespoke models, situating facilities in low‑population or repurposed industrial sites, and ensuring clear benefits to the communities that host them could mitigate backlash while still delivering the economic upside.

The future of AI infrastructure in Australia hinges on aligning regulatory ambition, market realities, and public acceptance in a way that recognises both the opportunities and the responsibilities the technology entails.

stories.title: OpenAI Builds Energy Desk to Manage AI Data Centre Power Needs
stories.summary: OpenAI is standing up an internal energy desk with roles spanning power trading and clean energy procurement to manage electricity and natural gas exposure across its global data center portfolio. The move mirrors a similar energy-trading buildout at Meta and reflects hyperscalers taking direct control of power sourcing rather than relying solely on utilities and developers. The desk is intended to secure reliable, scalable, and cost-resilient supply for AI infrastructure.
stories.why_it_matters: AI operators are becoming energy market participants in their own right, which changes who buys power, how it is contracted, and how risk is priced. Utilities, traders, and independent power producers gain a sophisticated new counterparty, while rivals face pressure to build equivalent capabilities to compete for scarce capacity.
stories.content:
### Internalising Clean Energy Strategy

A second hire, the Clean Energy and New Technology Lead, sits within OpenAI’s Industrial Compute organisation, which oversees site selection and buildout. This role will evaluate clean power, advanced storage, grid flexibility, and low-carbon backup technologies, focusing on their repeatable deployment across OpenAI’s growing campus footprint. Industry observers, such as Neil Osnato, founder of Persistence Analytics Group, highlight that this internalisation of emerging energy strategy within the buildout organisation suggests a desire to assess deployable power architectures project by project.This approach is evident in projects like Project Camellia, OpenAI’s planned 3.2 gigawatt (GW) campus in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company has committed to providing Georgia Power with up to 1,000 megawatts (MW) of flexible demand response under a 25-year agreement. The move to internalise energy management comes after OpenAI reportedly paused its Stargate UK project due to energy costs and regulatory hurdles, with Microsoft subsequently taking over capacity at the Stargate Norway site.

### Implications for India's Digital Infrastructure

This global trend by hyperscalers like OpenAI and Meta in directly managing energy for data centres will influence India's digital infrastructure and AI compute development, impacting power procurement strategies for Indian operators and investors. The focus on clean energy and grid flexibility for large-scale AI campuses could inform India's policy on renewable energy integration and grid infrastructure for future data centre parks. Lessons from stalled projects like Stargate due to energy costs highlight the importance of robust power strategies for hyperscaler expansions, a critical consideration for India's growing data centre market.The internalisation of energy expertise supports OpenAI’s January pledge to “pay its own way on energy,” providing the operational machinery needed to navigate diverse grid conditions and market volatilities. This strategic shift by major AI companies could set a precedent for Google, Microsoft, and Amazon, influencing their future commitments to gigawatt-scale data centre campuses and their ability to mitigate energy market risks.

stories.title: Solid-State Transformers Emerge for Next-Gen AI Data Centers
stories.summary: Solid-state transformers are emerging as a key enabling technology for high-voltage direct current architectures in next-generation AI data centers, offering improved efficiency and power conversion flexibility over conventional transformers. Proponents see SSTs as central to handling multi-megawatt racks and 800V DC distribution. Questions remain around technology maturity, cost, and supply chain readiness.
stories.why_it_matters: As rack densities outrun what conventional AC distribution can deliver efficiently, power electronics like SSTs will determine how next-generation facilities are designed and who supplies them. Early movers among vendors and operators could lock in architectural advantages, but adoption risk stays high until the technology proves out at scale.
stories.content:
Solid-state transformers (SSTs) are emerging as a cornerstone for high-voltage direct current (HVDC) architectures in high-density artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, promising enhanced efficiency and flexibility. The technology aims to address the growing power demands of AI infrastructure, though concerns about maturity and supply chain remain.

Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google

Highlights

Solid-state transformers (SSTs) are emerging as key for high-voltage direct current (HVDC) in AI data centers.

SSTs offer smaller footprints, higher efficiency, and bidirectional power flow compared to traditional transformers.

Silicon carbide (SiC) semiconductors enable SSTs to handle higher voltages and temperatures with improved efficiency.

Industry experts anticipate most new data centers will adopt SSTs by 2028, with hyperscalers leading deployment by 2027.

Solid-state transformers (SSTs) are gaining traction as a foundational technology for high-voltage direct current (HVDC) architectures within next-generation, high-density artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. This shift is driven by the increasing rack densities of AI workloads, which are pushing the adoption of HVDC internally, despite most external distribution grids still relying on alternating current (AC).Moving key power conversion stages from AC to DC can reduce equipment footprints, decrease weight, improve efficiency, enhance control, and simplify the integration of renewable energy sources like solar and battery storage.

SST Functionality and Benefits

SSTs are power electronics-based systems designed to condition and convert grid AC to DC. Unlike traditional low-frequency iron-core transformers, SSTs utilise high-frequency magnetics combined with semiconductor switching stages, resulting in smaller and lighter units. These systems can directly feed DC into a data center or convert back to AC if a site maintains an AC-native infrastructure.Beyond their compact form, SSTs enable bidirectional power flow, facilitating the integration of onsite solar and battery energy storage. They also offer power conditioning capabilities, filtering electrical noise and mitigating voltage and current oscillations while tailoring voltage to different loads. Most designs incorporate galvanic isolation through their high-frequency transformer stage and integrate advanced protection and control mechanisms.

Silicon Carbide's Role

Silicon carbide (SiC) semiconductors are critical for SST applications due to their ability to tolerate higher voltages and temperatures, alongside faster switching speeds compared to traditional silicon devices. This translates into reduced losses at high power levels, leading to higher efficiency, more compact form factors, and potentially shorter lead times for SSTs compared with conventional large transformers, which can take multiple years for delivery.

Direct MV-to-800 V DC for AI Loads

SSTs typically connect to medium-voltage (MV) AC distribution, such as 15 kV or 35 kV, and convert it to an 800 V DC bus for facility distribution. Many platforms support bidirectional power flow, allowing for import and export to support the grid, which is increasingly important given concerns around voltage transients in AI data centers. The 800 V DC bus is then often converted at the rack or sled level to 48 V for server power rails, aligning with modern AI chassis power architectures.Waqas Arshad, vice president of product and technology, microgrid solutions, at Delta, a manufacturer of SSTs, stated that power delivery has become a performance bottleneck, fueling the conversion to 800 V DC distribution. He added that SiC chips and control software have matured enough to make this type of MV-to-DC conversion practical at scale and with the necessary reliability. Delta's SST platform reportedly converts MV AC (6.6-35 kV) directly to 800 V DC at up to 98.5% efficiency, developed alongside Open Compute Project (OCP) efforts and Nvidia’s 800 V DC specification. Delta has reported dozens of units deployed in Asia and customer pilots underway in the US.Rick Sander, chief executive officer (CEO) of Alderbuck Energy, an electrical infrastructure and SST supplier, recommends SSTs for greenfield builds and AI retrofits. Alderbuck's Nexus Power Unit is positioned as a software-defined platform that replaces multiple pieces of conventional gear, including transformers, rectifiers, and inverters, with direct MV-to-HVDC conversion. This aims to reduce footprint, installation time, and energy losses. The company is piloting its technology at the San Diego Supercomputer Center at UC San Diego. Sander anticipates that most new data center installations will incorporate SSTs by 2028, with most data centers relying exclusively on SSTs by 2035.

Risks and Alternatives

Despite the potential, some industry experts advise caution regarding widespread SST deployment. Clayton Gibbons, head of power systems at SPOC Energy, a power-conversion system manufacturer, argues that SST technology still lacks the maturity and supply-chain depth required for a broad rollout. He proposes transformer-plus-rectifier approaches as an alternative path to 800 V DC, which he claims can achieve approximately 97.3% grid-to-rack efficiency while leveraging the existing MV transformer supply chain.Hitachi Energy also urges caution, with Vishak Gopinath, a spokesperson, noting that operating at 34.5 kV while maintaining compact designs introduces significant manufacturing and design challenges. Compact SSTs necessitate stringent insulation systems and high manufacturing quality to ensure a 20-year service life. Hitachi Energy continues to invest in SST building blocks, including MV converters, transformer design, MV SiC semiconductors, and low-voltage converter products.Shen Wang, partner at Fortune Virtue Capital and former practice lead for global data center infrastructure research at Omdia, expects a phased adoption, from AC-native designs to 400 V DC and then 800 V DC configurations over the next one to two years, led by hyperscalers. Scaled SST deployments are projected to become more common by 2027, particularly among hyperscalers and cloud service providers.

stories.title: SLB's $4.1 Billion Kelvion Deal Boosts AI Data Centre Cooling
stories.summary: SLB, the energy services company formerly known as Schlumberger, has agreed to acquire thermal management specialist Kelvion for $4.1 billion, expanding its data center business into cooling and heat rejection. The acquisition targets the escalating heat loads generated by high-density AI racks. Kelvion brings heat exchanger and cooling technologies that complement SLB's existing digital and infrastructure offerings.
stories.why_it_matters: A major oilfield services player paying billions for a cooling firm confirms thermal management is now a strategic, consolidating market driven by AI density. Data center operators should expect more integrated cooling offerings and fewer independent suppliers, reshaping procurement and technology roadmaps.
stories.content:
SLB is set to acquire thermal management firm Kelvion for $4.1 billion, significantly expanding its data centre business into cooling and heat rejection technologies. This strategic move directly addresses the escalating power densities and cooling demands driven by AI workloads in modern data centres.

Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google

Highlights

SLB to acquire Kelvion for $4.1 billion, significantly expanding its data centre thermal management capabilities.

The deal addresses escalating cooling demands from high-density AI workloads, pushing rack power densities above 100 kW.

Kelvion brings expertise in heat exchangers and heat rejection, including waterless cooling solutions.

SLB aims to integrate Kelvion's thermal technologies into its modular infrastructure, targeting over $2 billion revenue by 2026.

SLB, a technology company, will acquire thermal management specialist Kelvion for $4.1 billion, aiming to strengthen its data centre business by integrating advanced cooling and heat rejection capabilities. The acquisition positions SLB to meet the rising demands for thermal management solutions, particularly as artificial intelligence (AI) workloads drive higher power densities in data centres.The deal, valued at approximately $3.4 billion in cash and the assumption of $700 million in Kelvion debt, is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals. According to SLB, Kelvion's addition will more than double its revenue opportunity per gigawatt of delivered data centre capacity. The combined data centre business is projected to exceed $2 billion in revenue by 2026, with a target of $4.5 billion to $5 billion by 2028.

Addressing AI Cooling Demands

The acquisition brings Kelvion's expertise in heat exchangers, heat rejection equipment, and other thermal management technologies to SLB's existing capabilities in engineering, modular manufacturing, and power integration. This is particularly relevant as modern graphics processing units (GPUs) push rack power densities above 100 kW, with some future chip architectures potentially approaching 1 MW, significantly increasing the heat cooling systems must manage.Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell’Oro Group, noted that while much attention has focused on direct-to-chip cooling technologies, the segment experiencing the fastest repricing is heat rejection. Kelvion's technologies, including dry coolers and hybrid or adiabatic systems, are critical for addressing challenges such as rising rack densities and pressure on data centre water consumption. Kelvion also offers solutions for waterless cooling applications, providing options for markets with water availability constraints or community opposition to conventional cooling.

Integrated Infrastructure Strategy

SLB plans to integrate Kelvion’s thermal technologies directly into its modular infrastructure, shifting from a model where cooling is added as a separate system. Gavin Rennick, president of SLB’s New Energy and Industrial business, stated that this approach creates a more integrated infrastructure architecture, aligning performance requirements, configuration choices, and deployment timing for customers. SLB cited its role as a modular design partner for Nvidia AI factories as an example where Kelvion’s expertise could optimise cooling during design and fabrication.Cordovil emphasised that durable competitive advantage will depend on SLB’s ability to integrate these systems, rather than just manufacturing components. He also highlighted that Kelvion supplies components to other thermal management companies, meaning SLB could become both a competitor and a supplier within parts of the ecosystem.

Market Expansion and Future Opportunities

The acquisition also expands SLB’s geographic footprint. While SLB’s data centre business has primarily focused on the US, Kelvion has established operations and customers in Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. SLB CEO Olivier Le Peuch indicated that the US would remain foundational, followed by Europe, and then Asia and the Middle East.Beyond cooling, SLB views the acquisition as a potential entry point into other areas of the data centre infrastructure stack, including integrated power solutions such as behind-the-meter generation, geothermal, and carbon capture. Le Peuch suggested opportunities to offer hyperscalers integrated power, cooling, and modular infrastructure to support large AI deployments.

stories.title: OpenAI Secures $5.5 Billion in SB Energy Warrants for AI Data Centers
stories.summary: OpenAI has obtained warrants valued at roughly $5.5 billion in SB Energy, the SoftBank-backed power infrastructure company, to underpin its AI data center buildout. The position follows a separate $1.5 billion investment in SB Energy by Nvidia, concentrating chipmaker and model developer capital in the same power platform. The structure ties compute demand directly to dedicated generation and infrastructure development.
stories.why_it_matters: AI labs and their hardware suppliers are now financing the power layer of the stack, not just servers and buildings. This vertical alignment accelerates project delivery for OpenAI's Stargate-scale ambitions while concentrating influence over new generation capacity in the hands of a few AI players.
stories.content:
OpenAI has secured warrants worth an estimated $5.5 billion in SB Energy, a power infrastructure firm, to support its AI data center expansion. This move follows a $1.5 billion investment by Nvidia in SB Energy, signaling a concerted effort to build dedicated infrastructure for AI workloads.

Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google

Highlights

OpenAI secured $5.5 billion in warrants from SB Energy for AI data center expansion.

Nvidia invested $1.5 billion in SB Energy and guaranteed $105 billion for an Ohio data center lease.

SB Energy and OpenAI plan to be key tenants in three new AI-focused data centers.

SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary, builds large-scale power and data center infrastructure.

OpenAI has secured warrants worth approximately $5.5 billion in SB Energy, a power infrastructure firm, as part of a strategic push into dedicated data center capacity for artificial intelligence (AI) workloads. This development, reported by the Wall Street Journal, indicates a significant investment in the energy infrastructure required to power advanced AI systems.Earlier this month, Nvidia also invested $1.5 billion in SB Energy. Additionally, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion to facilitate OpenAI's lease of a data center in Ohio being developed by SB Energy. These investments underscore the rising capital expenditure in power and data center infrastructure necessary for scaling AI compute capabilities.

AI Data Center Expansion

SoftBank Group and OpenAI are designated tenants in three new data centers being developed by SB Energy. These facilities are specifically designed to meet the increasing demands of AI, highlighting a trend towards purpose-built infrastructure for high-density AI compute. SB Energy, a subsidiary of SoftBank, is actively developing large-scale power and data center infrastructure projects, including several data center campuses to support the growth of AI workloads.

Market Implications

The substantial investments by OpenAI and Nvidia in SB Energy suggest a strategic alignment between AI developers, chipmakers, and power infrastructure providers. This collaboration is crucial for ensuring the availability of reliable and scalable energy resources for next-generation AI data centers. SB Energy is reportedly seeking a valuation exceeding $50 billion in its potential market debut, which could occur as early as next month, according to Reuters sources earlier this year. This valuation reflects the growing investor interest in companies positioned to enable the expansion of AI infrastructure.
